method: All 240 exact propositions and retained numerical rationales reviewed for each of eight profiles. Unknowns checked against available source scope; no filling from adjacent claims. Core Oxford, Hobhouse, TRG, GOP, NatCon, Australian platform, Thatcher and Brookings sources re-read. No score targets consulted.
sourceAccessNotes: Liberal International and TRG web renderer timed out; Oxford cached full HTML and freshly curl-fetched TRG HTML were read.
Modern government source coverage remains limited to the specified profile periods and contextual acts; this review is not a new comprehensive incumbent-government survey.

findings.question: Essential utility networks in my country, such as water supply networks, should be publicly owned.
findings.reason: Oxford II.1 permits public ownership only in specified circumstances; that necessary condition does not recommend public ownership of every network monopoly. No sector-specific preference is established.

findings.question: Passenger rail infrastructure in my country should be publicly owned.
findings.reason: Oxford II.1 permits public ownership only in specified circumstances; that necessary condition does not recommend public ownership of every network monopoly. No sector-specific preference is established.

findings.question: My country should provide a stronger minimum income through benefits, even when this requires higher taxes.
findings.reason: Oxford I.3 promises security against sickness, unemployment, disability and old age. It does not specify the cash-benefit level, tax trade-off or eligibility boundary in this question.

findings.question: People eligible for income benefits should receive enough support to participate in ordinary social life, beyond meeting basic survival needs.
findings.reason: Oxford I.3 promises security against sickness, unemployment, disability and old age. It does not specify the cash-benefit level, tax trade-off or eligibility boundary in this question.

findings.question: Cash benefits should be restricted to households unable to meet basic needs rather than extended to a wider range of low-income households.
findings.reason: Oxford I.3 promises security against sickness, unemployment, disability and old age. It does not specify the cash-benefit level, tax trade-off or eligibility boundary in this question.

findings.question: My country’s laws should be justified without relying on the teachings of any particular religion.
findings.reason: Oxford protects worship and conscience without specifying this state-religion institution. Religious freedom alone does not establish strict separation, marriage procedures, clerical legislative seats or civil-court exclusivity.

findings.question: Religious teachings should be an official source of national law in my country.
findings.reason: Oxford protects worship and conscience without specifying this state-religion institution. Religious freedom alone does not establish strict separation, marriage procedures, clerical legislative seats or civil-court exclusivity.

findings.question: My government should make policy without needing approval from religious leaders.
findings.reason: Oxford protects worship and conscience without specifying this state-religion institution. Religious freedom alone does not establish strict separation, marriage procedures, clerical legislative seats or civil-court exclusivity.

findings.question: Public schools in my country should include instruction intended to cultivate faith in the state’s recognised religion.
findings.reason: Oxford protects worship and conscience without specifying this state-religion institution. Religious freedom alone does not establish strict separation, marriage procedures, clerical legislative seats or civil-court exclusivity.

findings.question: My country’s state courts should apply laws enacted by civil institutions rather than rulings issued by religious authorities.
findings.reason: Oxford protects worship and conscience without specifying this state-religion institution. Religious freedom alone does not establish strict separation, marriage procedures, clerical legislative seats or civil-court exclusivity.

findings.question: Religious leaders should not hold government seats solely because of their religious office.
findings.reason: Oxford protects worship and conscience without specifying this state-religion institution. Religious freedom alone does not establish strict separation, marriage procedures, clerical legislative seats or civil-court exclusivity.

findings.question: My country should remove religious approval requirements from laws governing marriage.
findings.reason: Oxford protects worship and conscience without specifying this state-religion institution. Religious freedom alone does not establish strict separation, marriage procedures, clerical legislative seats or civil-court exclusivity.

findings.question: Adults who take on roles traditionally associated with the other sex should receive the same social acceptance as those who follow traditional roles.
findings.reason: Equality of legal rights between men and women is not a statement about equal social acceptance of every nontraditional role. The manifesto does not answer that social judgement.

findings.question: The government should recognise several cultural traditions as part of my country’s national identity.
findings.reason: Respect for national minorities and their customs does not itself prescribe incorporating several cultural traditions into the official national identity.

findings.question: My country’s national identity should include several distinct cultural ways of life.
findings.reason: Respect for national minorities and their customs does not itself prescribe incorporating several cultural traditions into the official national identity.

findings.question: Diplomatic measures should take priority over military action, even when they are slower to achieve my country’s aims.
findings.reason: The manifesto proposes international peace and enforceable common obligations; it does not settle this specific military-versus-diplomatic sacrifice or negotiated capability reduction.

findings.question: My country should leave a territorial dispute unresolved rather than start a war to settle it.
findings.reason: The manifesto proposes international peace and enforceable common obligations; it does not settle this specific military-versus-diplomatic sacrifice or negotiated capability reduction.

findings.question: My country should accept reductions in its military capabilities as part of negotiated efforts to prevent war.
findings.reason: The manifesto proposes international peace and enforceable common obligations; it does not settle this specific military-versus-diplomatic sacrifice or negotiated capability reduction.

findings.question: Elected representatives should be able to remove the head of government for serious abuse of power through a defined constitutional process.
findings.reason: General democratic accountability does not prescribe parliamentary removal of the executive through the specific constitutional process asked here.

findings.question: Voters should be able to repeal a law through a binding referendum.
findings.reason: Hobhouse pp.245–248 proposes referring a disputed bill to voters before enactment, at government discretion. This does not establish a popular right to repeal an existing law through a binding referendum.

findings.question: My country should establish publicly owned businesses in competitive industries rather than leave those industries entirely to private owners.
findings.reason: Hobhouse supports collective provision for monopoly or unmet social functions. That does not establish a preference for starting public businesses in otherwise competitive industries.

findings.question: Businesses extracting natural resources in my country should generally be publicly owned.
findings.reason: Recovering socially created resource rents through taxation or public control does not determine ownership of extraction businesses themselves.

findings.question: My government should subsidise selected industries to steer economic development, even when private investors would favour other sectors.
findings.reason: Public investment and social provision do not establish subsidies to selected industries against private investment preferences. The earlier rationale described a possibility rather than a sourced recommendation.

findings.question: State and local governments should keep most of the tax revenue collected in their area rather than send it to the national government to allocate.
findings.reason: National social provision does not establish whether local governments should retain most locally collected taxes. The quantitative revenue-allocation choice remains unsupported.

findings.question: My country should use taxes and benefits to substantially reduce differences in disposable income.
findings.reason: TRG compassion, welfare reform and fair society commitments do not establish this exact cash-transfer level or disposable-income equalisation objective. The earlier rationale supplied an assumed mechanism.

findings.question: My country should provide a stronger minimum income through benefits, even when this requires higher taxes.
findings.reason: TRG compassion, welfare reform and fair society commitments do not establish this exact cash-transfer level or disposable-income equalisation objective. The earlier rationale supplied an assumed mechanism.

findings.question: People eligible for income benefits should receive enough support to participate in ordinary social life, beyond meeting basic survival needs.
findings.reason: TRG compassion, welfare reform and fair society commitments do not establish this exact cash-transfer level or disposable-income equalisation objective. The earlier rationale supplied an assumed mechanism.

findings.question: My country should remove religious approval requirements from laws governing marriage.
findings.reason: Availability of civil marriage in Britain is not evidence that this scoped One Nation doctrine recommends removing religious approval conditions from marriage law.

findings.question: Choosing an abortion early in pregnancy should be socially accepted.
findings.reason: The 2024 platform explicitly opposes late-term abortion and supports state decision-making; neither establishes its position on social acceptance of early-pregnancy abortion in this question.

findings.question: My government should direct investment towards sectors chosen in a national economic plan.
findings.reason: Tariffs and restoring manufacturing capacity are not an economy-wide investment plan directing private capital. The platform does not specify the proposed planning instrument.

findings.question: My government should subsidise selected industries to steer economic development, even when private investors would favour other sectors.
findings.reason: Tariff protection and deregulation do not by themselves establish subsidies to selected industries against private investors’ preferences.

findings.question: My country should allow more migrants from diverse backgrounds because their cultures differ from our own.
findings.reason: The programme prioritises national integration, but not making diversity an admission objective is not equivalent to opposing the precise proposal to encourage culturally different settlement.

findings.question: Long-standing customs should be preserved for their connection to earlier generations, even when their practical purpose is no longer clear.
findings.reason: Celebrating national heritage does not establish preserving a custom even after its practical purpose becomes unclear. The stated qualifying trade-off is not addressed.

findings.question: Elected representatives should be able to remove the head of government for serious abuse of power through a defined constitutional process.
findings.reason: The previous rationale showed compatibility with constitutional democracy, not evidence for this precise parliamentary-removal mechanism. No specific institutional recommendation was cited.

findings.question: My country should make long-term commitments to international alliances, even when those commitments limit its freedom to act independently.
findings.reason: The Brookings account describes coalitions whose mission and terms are set by Washington and rejection of treaty restraints. Support for allies does not establish accepting long-term limits on independent action.

findings.question: Adults should be allowed to make personal choices such as drug use that risk personal wellbeing when they do not directly harm others.
findings.reason: The declaration criticises addictive substances for their effects on public life and families. This does not establish prohibition in the question’s expressly self-regarding case with no direct harm to others.

findings.question: Authorities should be able to prohibit a public gathering when there is credible evidence that it is likely to lead to serious disorder.
findings.reason: Stopping riots and looting after unlawful disorder is not a recommendation to prohibit a gathering in advance on evidence of likely disorder.

findings.question: Becoming part of the national community should not require giving up a foreign cultural identity.
findings.reason: Section4 expressly protects minority traditions and community institutions while section9 favours assimilation. Maintaining a foreign private heritage need not bar national membership; shared civic allegiance is required.

findings.question: The government should recognise several cultural traditions as part of my country’s national identity.
findings.reason: Protection of minority institutions does not specify recognition of several traditions within official national identity. No sourced neutral balance on this exact policy is established.

findings.question: My country’s national identity should include several distinct cultural ways of life.
findings.reason: The declaration protects communal minorities within a shared national culture; it does not settle whether the national identity itself should contain several cultural ways of life. Conditional private liberty is not a neutral answer to this identity proposition.

findings.question: My country should make long-term commitments to international alliances, even when those commitments limit its freedom to act independently.
findings.reason: Section2 expressly conditions defensive alliances on respecting member independence. It does not establish willingness to accept the question’s stated limits on independent action.

findings.question: The government should retain ownership of strategic businesses even when selling them would raise substantial public revenue.
findings.reason: Strategic independence can be achieved through regulation or domestic private ownership. It does not establish keeping strategic firms publicly owned despite revenue from sale.

findings.question: Official ceremonies held by my government should not include organised religious worship.
findings.reason: Section4 calls for public honouring of Christianity but does not specify organised worship in government ceremonies, symbols on government buildings or official religious festival holidays. These particular practices cannot be inferred from public religion alone.

findings.question: Government buildings should not display symbols endorsing a particular religion.
findings.reason: Section4 calls for public honouring of Christianity but does not specify organised worship in government ceremonies, symbols on government buildings or official religious festival holidays. These particular practices cannot be inferred from public religion alone.

findings.question: My country should keep national public holidays marking the predominant religion’s major festivals as an official recognition of that religion.
findings.reason: Section4 calls for public honouring of Christianity but does not specify organised worship in government ceremonies, symbols on government buildings or official religious festival holidays. These particular practices cannot be inferred from public religion alone.

findings.question: Language conventions should change to reflect how people identify themselves, even when this departs from traditional usage.
findings.reason: The declaration supports a traditional male-female family model, but does not address adapting pronouns or everyday language to a person’s self-description. The previous argument added a specific convention not present in the source.

findings.question: Schools should teach pupils about different sexual orientations and gender identities, even when these differ from traditional family expectations.
findings.reason: Parental authority and religious-community education rights do not settle whether schools may teach descriptive information about other orientations and identities. Opposition to sexual experimentation is not opposition to every informative lesson.

findings.question: States and regions should be able to adopt their own constitutions defining how their governments work, within the rights protected by the national constitution.
findings.reason: Federal delegation and regional variation do not establish a right to adopt separate regional constitutions. The precise institutional authority is unspecified.

findings.question: My country should remove religious approval requirements from laws governing marriage.
findings.reason: Neither freedom of belief nor Australia’s present civil-marriage arrangements establishes a doctrinal recommendation to remove religious marriage approval requirements.

findings.question: Adults who take on roles traditionally associated with the other sex should receive the same social acceptance as those who follow traditional roles.
findings.reason: A fair go and legal equality protect individual opportunities but do not explicitly require equal social acceptance of nontraditional sex roles.

findings.question: My government should subsidise selected industries to steer economic development, even when private investors would favour other sectors.
findings.reason: Strategic government and industry competitiveness do not establish a neutral policy on industry subsidies where private capital favours other sectors. The earlier public-benefit condition was supplied by the assessor.

findings.question: Authorities should be able to prohibit a public gathering when there is credible evidence that it is likely to lead to serious disorder.
findings.reason: The speech supports stronger policing and punishment of violent offences. It does not establish prohibiting a future gathering based on a risk of disorder.

findings.question: My country should maintain forces capable of prolonged combat beyond its borders.
findings.reason: Conventional and nuclear deterrence and support for NATO do not establish a preference for maintaining prolonged overseas combat capability. This particular capability needs separate evidence.

findings.question: My country should be willing to threaten military action to obtain concessions in serious international disputes.
findings.reason: Deterring aggression by military strength is not identical to threatening military action to obtain concessions in a dispute. The source does not establish the latter policy.

findings.question: My country should remove religious approval requirements from laws governing marriage.
findings.reason: Historical availability of civil marriage is not evidence of a specific Thatcherite recommendation on removing religious approval conditions.

findings.question: State and local governments should keep most of the tax revenue collected in their area rather than send it to the national government to allocate.
findings.reason: Parliamentary sovereignty and general fiscal restraint do not settle this specific distribution of local revenue, school-curriculum authority or control over council boundaries. No applicable act or explicit doctrinal passage was cited.

findings.question: The national government should decide what all school pupils must study, even if regions want different compulsory subjects.
findings.reason: Parliamentary sovereignty and general fiscal restraint do not settle this specific distribution of local revenue, school-curriculum authority or control over council boundaries. No applicable act or explicit doctrinal passage was cited.

findings.question: Local voters should be able to change the powers and boundaries of their councils without national approval.
findings.reason: Parliamentary sovereignty and general fiscal restraint do not settle this specific distribution of local revenue, school-curriculum authority or control over council boundaries. No applicable act or explicit doctrinal passage was cited.
